texts.title: Why I stopped planning every minute

segments.speaker: Host
segments.text: Today we are talking to travel writer Maya Chen, who recently published an article about unplanned travel. Maya, you used to organize every trip in great detail. What changed?

segments.speaker: Maya
segments.text: I missed a train in northern Spain three years ago. At first I was furious because my timetable was ruined. But I ended up spending six hours in a town I had never heard of. I found a small market, spoke to a family who ran a bakery, and learned more about the area than I probably would have on my original route.

segments.speaker: Host
segments.text: So now you avoid planning?

segments.speaker: Maya
segments.text: Not completely. I still book accommodation for the first night and check safety information. What changed is that I no longer fill every hour. I leave space for delays, recommendations and conversations. That makes a trip less efficient, but often more memorable.

segments.speaker: Host
segments.text: Some people would say that approach is only possible if you have extra time and money.

segments.speaker: Maya
segments.text: That criticism is fair. Flexibility can be a privilege. If you have a strict work schedule, children with you, or a limited budget, missing a train can be a serious problem rather than an adventure. I think the lesson is not that everyone should travel spontaneously. It is simply that perfect control is not always the same as a good experience.

questions.prompt: What event changed Maya's approach to travel?
options: She stayed in an expensive hotel.
questions.explanationJa: きっかけはスペイン北部で列車に乗り遅れたことです。

questions.prompt: Give two things Maya did during the unexpected six-hour stop.
markscheme: She visited a small market.
She spoke to a family who ran a bakery and/or learned more about the local area.
questions.explanationJa: 市場を訪れたことと、パン屋を営む家族と話したことが中心です。

questions.prompt: Complete the idea: Maya still books accommodation for the ________ night.
markscheme: first
questions.explanationJa: すべてを無計画にするのではなく、最初の夜の宿は予約します。

questions.prompt: What does Maya now deliberately leave in her schedule?
options: Space for unexpected events and recommendations
questions.explanationJa: delays、recommendations、conversationsのための余白を残します。

questions.prompt: Choose TWO situations that Maya says can make flexibility difficult.
questions.explanationJa: 仕事の厳しい日程と、子ども連れの旅行を具体例として挙げています。

questions.prompt: What is Maya's final point?
options: People should never make travel plans.
Perfect control does not necessarily create the best experience.
Travellers should spend more money for flexibility.
questions.explanationJa: 『完全に管理すること＝良い経験』とは限らない、という結論です。

segments.speaker: Reporter
segments.text: The central library in Brookdale will begin opening until midnight during examination season after a six-month student campaign. Until now, the building has closed at eight in the evening.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: A lot of students live in crowded homes or share bedrooms with younger brothers and sisters. We were not asking for luxury. We wanted a quiet, safe place to work after dinner.

segments.speaker: Reporter
segments.text: The council originally rejected the idea because keeping the entire building open would require extra security and cleaning staff. The revised plan uses only the ground floor after ten o'clock and limits late opening to the four weeks before major exams.

segments.speaker: Librarian
segments.text: We will also require students under sixteen to leave by ten unless they are accompanied by an adult. That rule disappointed some campaigners, but we have to balance access with safeguarding.

segments.speaker: Reporter
segments.text: The trial will begin next month. The council says it will review attendance, staffing costs and reports from nearby residents before deciding whether the extended hours should return next year.

questions.prompt: What change will the library make during examination season?
options: It will open earlier in the morning.
It will remain open until midnight.
It will close the ground floor.
questions.explanationJa: 試験期に限り深夜0時まで開館します。

questions.prompt: Give two reasons students wanted later opening hours.
markscheme: Some students live in crowded homes or share rooms.
They wanted a quiet and safe place to study after dinner.
questions.explanationJa: 家庭で静かな学習場所を確保しにくいことと、安全で静かな場所が必要なことです。

questions.prompt: Why did the council reject the original plan?
options: The library had too few books.
Opening the whole building would increase staffing costs.
questions.explanationJa: securityとcleaningの追加人員が必要になるためです。

questions.prompt: Choose TWO features of the revised plan.
options: Only the ground floor stays open after 10 p.m.
Late opening is limited to four weeks before major exams.
All students may remain until midnight without restrictions.
The library closes at 6 p.m. on weekends.
questions.explanationJa: 22時以降は1階のみ、そして主要試験前の4週間に限定されます。

questions.prompt: Students under sixteen must leave by ten unless they are with an ________.
markscheme: adult
questions.explanationJa: 16歳未満はadult同伴でなければ22時までです。

questions.prompt: What will the council examine after the trial?
options: Attendance, staffing costs and residents' reports
questions.explanationJa: attendance、staffing costs、nearby residentsからの報告を確認します。

segments.speaker: Moderator
segments.text: Our final topic is smartphone design. Engineer Daniel Brooks, why are so many phones difficult to repair?

segments.speaker: Daniel
segments.text: There is no single reason. Consumers want thin devices that resist water, and manufacturers want fast assembly. Glue can help with both goals, but it also makes batteries and screens harder to replace.

segments.speaker: Moderator
segments.text: Campaigner Sara Malik, what would you change?

segments.speaker: Sara
segments.text: I would require companies to sell spare parts for a reasonable number of years and publish repair instructions. I would also like batteries to be easier to replace. A phone should not become electronic waste simply because one component has worn out.

segments.speaker: Daniel
segments.text: I support better access to parts, but we should be careful. Some repairs involve damaged batteries, and poor work can create a fire risk. We need products that are repairable, but we also need clear warnings about which jobs require trained technicians.

segments.speaker: Sara
segments.text: That's true. Right-to-repair does not mean everyone must repair everything themselves. It means the owner should have a realistic choice: repair it personally if the task is simple, use an independent technician, or return it to the manufacturer.

segments.speaker: Moderator
segments.text: So perhaps the debate is less about whether repair matters and more about how to make repair practical without ignoring safety.

questions.prompt: According to Daniel, why is glue used in some phones?
options: It makes phones cheaper to recycle.
It can help make phones thin and water-resistant.
It makes batteries safer to remove.
questions.explanationJa: 薄型化と耐水性に役立つ一方、修理を難しくします。

questions.prompt: Give two changes Sara wants manufacturers to make.
markscheme: Sell spare parts for a reasonable number of years and/or publish repair instructions.
Make batteries easier to replace.
questions.explanationJa: spare parts、repair instructions、交換しやすいbatteryのうち2点です。

questions.prompt: Choose TWO concerns Daniel raises about repair.
options: Damaged batteries can create fire risks.
questions.explanationJa: battery fire riskと、trained technicianが必要な作業の存在です。

questions.prompt: Sara says the owner should have a realistic ________.
markscheme: choice
questions.explanationJa: repair方法を選べる現実的なchoiceが必要だと述べています。

questions.prompt: According to Sara, what are two possible repair routes for an owner?
markscheme: Repair the product personally if the task is simple.
Use an independent technician and/or return it to the manufacturer.
questions.explanationJa: 自分で修理、独立系技術者、メーカーへ戻す、のうち2つです。

questions.prompt: How does the moderator summarize the discussion?
options: Repair is unnecessary for modern phones.
Safety is more important than repair in every case.
The challenge is making repair practical while protecting safety.
questions.explanationJa: repairabilityとsafetyの両立が中心論点だとまとめています。

texts.title: The name I use at work

segments.speaker: Speaker
segments.text: When I started my first weekend job, I introduced myself as Sam instead of Sameer. Nobody asked me to change my name. I simply thought Sam would be easier for customers and colleagues to remember.

segments.speaker: Speaker
segments.text: At first the decision felt practical, but after a few months I noticed something uncomfortable. People at work knew a version of me that my family never used. When a colleague finally heard my mother call me Sameer, she laughed and said, 'I didn't know that was your real name.' She meant no harm, but the comment stayed with me.

segments.speaker: Speaker
segments.text: I began wondering why one name had started to feel more official than the other. Sam was not fake; friends genuinely used it. But Sameer carried family history, and I did not like the idea that convenience should make that history disappear.

segments.speaker: Speaker
segments.text: Eventually I changed my work name badge to 'Sameer — Sam'. It created a few more questions, but most were friendly. More importantly, I stopped feeling that I had to choose between making communication easy and keeping a visible connection to my background.

questions.prompt: Why did Sameer initially use the name Sam at work?
options: He thought it would be easier for others to remember.
He wanted a completely new identity.
questions.explanationJa: 職場で覚えてもらいやすいという実用的な理由でした。

questions.prompt: Give two reasons the colleague's comment affected him.
markscheme: It suggested that Sameer was his 'real' name while Sam was somehow less real or vice versa, making him question which identity seemed official.
Sameer was connected to family history and he did not want convenience to erase that connection.
questions.explanationJa: nameの『本物らしさ』とfamily historyへのつながりが問題になりました。

questions.prompt: Sameer says that Sam was not ________.
markscheme: fake
questions.explanationJa: Samも実際に友人が使う名前なのでfakeではありません。

questions.prompt: Choose TWO results of changing the badge to 'Sameer — Sam'.
options: It created a few more questions.
His family asked him to quit.
questions.explanationJa: 質問は増えましたが、その多くはfriendlyでした。

questions.prompt: What conflict did the new badge help him avoid?
options: Choosing between easy communication and visible cultural connection
Choosing whether to see his family
questions.explanationJa: communicationの便利さとbackgroundへのvisible connectionを二者択一にしなくてよくなりました。

questions.prompt: What is the main focus of the essay?
options: How names can connect convenience, identity and family history
Why everyone should use a nickname
Why workplaces should ban name badges
questions.explanationJa: 名前を通じたidentityとfamily history、実用性の関係が主題です。

texts.title: The school that cut food waste

segments.speaker: Interviewer
segments.text: Your school says it has reduced cafeteria food waste by almost forty percent. What was the first step?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: We measured the waste for two weeks. Students were surprised by the amount of unopened food being thrown away. Before changing the menu, we needed to know what the problem actually was.

segments.speaker: Interviewer
segments.text: What changes followed?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: We introduced two portion sizes and allowed students to take fruit at the end of lunch instead of automatically placing it on every tray. We also moved one unpopular meal from a weekly to a monthly schedule.

segments.speaker: Interviewer
segments.text: Did students simply get less food?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: No. Anyone can ask for a second serving of the main dish if food is available. The goal is not smaller meals; it is matching portions to appetite. We also donate safe unopened items to a local community kitchen.

segments.speaker: Interviewer
segments.text: What remains difficult?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Special events. On sports days and festivals, attendance is harder to predict, so we still prepare too much sometimes. Our next step is to improve forecasting rather than pretending waste can be eliminated completely.

questions.prompt: What did the school do before changing the menu?
options: It measured food waste for two weeks.
questions.explanationJa: まず2週間、実際のwaste量を測定しました。

questions.prompt: Give two changes the school made to normal lunches.
markscheme: It introduced two portion sizes.
Students could take fruit later rather than receiving it automatically and/or an unpopular meal was served less often.
questions.explanationJa: portion size、fruitの配布方法、人気の低いmenu頻度の変更です。

questions.prompt: Choose TWO statements that are true about the new system.
options: Students can request a second serving when food is available.
Safe unopened items may be donated.
The school now serves only small meals.
questions.explanationJa: second servingとsafe unopened foodのdonationが正しいです。

questions.prompt: The goal is to match portions to students' ________.
markscheme: appetite
questions.explanationJa: portionをappetiteに合わせることが目的です。

questions.prompt: Why are special events still difficult?
questions.explanationJa: sports dayやfestivalではattendance予測が難しいためです。

questions.prompt: What is the school's next priority?
questions.explanationJa: 次の重点はforecasting改善です。

segments.speaker: Moderator
segments.text: Our final debate asks whether the voting age in local elections should be lowered to sixteen. Councillor Reed, you support the change.

segments.speaker: Reed
segments.text: Yes. Sixteen-year-olds work, pay taxes in some cases, use public transport, attend schools funded by local government and are affected by decisions about housing and climate. If politics concerns their lives, they should have a formal voice.

segments.speaker: Moderator
segments.text: Dr Patel, you disagree.

segments.speaker: Patel
segments.text: I am not against youth participation. My concern is consistency. At sixteen, many legal responsibilities are still limited. Before changing the voting age, we should ask why this particular right should move earlier while others do not.

segments.speaker: Reed
segments.text: But rights do not all begin at the same age now. We already use different ages for driving, employment and other responsibilities. The important question is whether sixteen-year-olds can make a meaningful political choice, not whether every law uses one birthday.

segments.speaker: Patel
segments.text: Then civic education becomes crucial. Lowering the age without helping young people understand local institutions may change the number of voters without improving participation. Schools would need time and resources to teach how councils actually work.

segments.speaker: Reed
segments.text: I agree with the education point. In fact, allowing students to vote while they are still in school could make civic education more relevant because the knowledge would have an immediate purpose.

segments.speaker: Moderator
segments.text: So although you disagree on the voting age, both of you see civic education as part of the issue.

questions.prompt: What is Reed's main argument for lowering the voting age?
options: Local political decisions already affect young people's lives.
All legal rights should begin at sixteen.
Young people pay more tax than adults.
questions.explanationJa: local governmentの決定が若者の生活に直接影響するため、formal voiceを持つべきだという主張です。

questions.prompt: Give two examples Reed uses to show that local politics affects sixteen-year-olds.
markscheme: They use public transport and/or attend schools funded by local government.
They are affected by decisions about housing and/or climate; some also work or pay taxes.
questions.explanationJa: public transport、school funding、housing、climate、work/taxなどから2点です。

questions.prompt: Choose TWO points made by Patel.
options: Many legal responsibilities are still limited at sixteen.
Civic education would need time and resources.
All rights must begin at exactly the same age.
questions.explanationJa: 16歳では法的責任が一部限定される点と、civic educationにresourceが必要な点です。

questions.prompt: Reed says rights do not all begin at the same ________.
markscheme: age
questions.explanationJa: rightsは現在もすべて同じageから始まるわけではないと述べます。

questions.prompt: Why does Reed think voting at sixteen could strengthen civic education? Give two linked ideas.
markscheme: Students would be able to vote while they are still in school.
The knowledge taught in civic education would have an immediate practical purpose and therefore feel more relevant.
questions.explanationJa: school在学中に実際に投票できれば、学んだ内容にimmediate purposeが生まれるという論理です。

questions.prompt: What area of agreement does the moderator identify?
options: The voting age should definitely be sixteen.
Civic education is an important part of the debate.
Young people should vote only at school.
questions.explanationJa: voting age自体では対立しますが、civic educationの重要性では一致しています。

segments.speaker: Host
segments.text: Our guest today is architecture student Lina Ortiz, who recently wrote about changing the way she speaks in different situations. Lina, when did you first become aware of your accent?

segments.speaker: Lina
segments.text: Probably in secondary school. At home I spoke English with the rhythm and expressions I had grown up with, but at school I started flattening certain sounds because classmates sometimes asked me to repeat myself even when they had understood perfectly well.

segments.speaker: Host
segments.text: Was that a deliberate decision?

segments.speaker: Lina
segments.text: Not at first. It was more like a habit that grew. Later, when I started giving presentations, I realized I was concentrating so hard on sounding neutral that I was speaking less naturally. I was choosing simpler words and avoiding jokes because I was worried that my pronunciation would draw attention.

segments.speaker: Host
segments.text: What changed your mind?

segments.speaker: Lina
segments.text: A lecturer told me that clarity mattered, but sameness did not. That sentence helped. I still slow down if a technical idea is difficult, and I repeat a word if someone genuinely misses it. But I no longer treat every sign of my background as a communication problem.

segments.speaker: Host
segments.text: So you would tell everyone never to adapt their speech?

segments.speaker: Lina
segments.text: No. Adapting can be useful and sometimes necessary. The difference for me is whether I am adapting to help communication or editing myself because I think one kind of English is automatically more acceptable than another.

questions.prompt: Why did Lina begin changing some sounds at school?
options: She wanted to become an actor.
Classmates sometimes asked her to repeat herself.
Her family told her to change her accent.
She was learning a third language.
questions.explanationJa: 同級生に繰り返すよう求められた経験がきっかけでした。

questions.prompt: Give two effects that trying to sound neutral had on Lina's presentations.
markscheme: She spoke less naturally and/or concentrated heavily on how she sounded.
She chose simpler words and/or avoided jokes.
questions.explanationJa: 自然さが失われ、語彙や冗談まで制限するようになりました。

questions.prompt: The lecturer told Lina that clarity mattered, but ________ did not.
markscheme: sameness
questions.explanationJa: 重要なのはclarityであり、全員が同じ話し方をすることではないという意味です。

questions.prompt: Choose TWO things Lina still does to support communication.
options: She slows down for difficult technical ideas.
She repeats a word if someone genuinely misses it.
She changes her name before presentations.
She removes every joke from her speech.
questions.explanationJa: 難しい技術的内容ではゆっくり話し、実際に聞き取れなかった場合は繰り返します。

questions.prompt: What distinction does Lina make at the end?
options: Useful adaptation and self-editing based on perceived acceptability
questions.explanationJa: communicationのためのadaptationと、受け入れられるよう自分を消すself-editingを区別しています。

questions.prompt: Which attitude best describes Lina's view of accent now?
options: She believes accents should never change.
She sees accent as part of identity but still values clear communication.
She thinks only one accent is professional.
She no longer cares whether listeners understand her.
questions.explanationJa: identityを保ちつつ、clarityのための調整は必要とするバランスの取れた立場です。

texts.title: What the night shift taught me

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: Eighteen-year-old Noah spent six weekends volunteering at a community emergency shelter. Noah, what surprised you most about the night shift?

segments.speaker: Noah
segments.text: I expected the difficult part to be staying awake. Actually, the harder part was not knowing whether someone wanted conversation or privacy. Some people arrived exhausted and wanted practical help immediately. Others wanted to tell the whole story of their day before they could settle.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: Did you receive training for that?

segments.speaker: Noah
segments.text: Yes, but training gave us principles, not scripts. We learned to ask simple questions, explain what we could and could not do, and avoid making promises. The experienced volunteers were especially good at leaving silence without making it feel awkward.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: Was there anything you found frustrating?

segments.speaker: Noah
segments.text: At first, yes. I wanted every shift to end with a visible success. But sometimes the useful thing was just finding a clean blanket, charging someone's phone, or giving accurate information about where to go the next morning. I had to stop measuring help by how dramatic it looked.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: Has the experience changed what you want to study?

segments.speaker: Noah
segments.text: Maybe. I am still interested in engineering, but now I am also curious about public services. The main change is that I pay more attention to systems people normally notice only when those systems fail.

questions.prompt: What did Noah find harder than staying awake?
options: Knowing whether people wanted conversation or privacy
questions.explanationJa: 相手が会話を望むのか、静かにしてほしいのか判断することが難しかったと述べています。

questions.prompt: Give two principles Noah learned in training.
markscheme: Ask simple questions and/or explain clearly what volunteers could and could not do.
Avoid making promises.
questions.explanationJa: simple questions、役割の範囲説明、promiseをしないことなどがtrainingの原則です。

questions.prompt: What skill did Noah admire in experienced volunteers?
options: Leaving silence without making it awkward
questions.explanationJa: 沈黙を無理に埋めず、それでも気まずくしない姿勢を評価しています。

questions.prompt: Choose TWO examples Noah gives of useful but undramatic help.
questions.explanationJa: clean blanketとphone chargingが具体例として挙げられています。

questions.prompt: Noah says he stopped measuring help by how ________ it looked.
markscheme: dramatic
questions.explanationJa: 目立つ成果だけをhelpと考えないようになった、という意味です。

questions.prompt: What is the main change Noah identifies at the end?
options: He now notices public systems people often take for granted.
He wants to become a night-shift manager immediately.
questions.explanationJa: 普段は意識されないpublic systemsに注意を向けるようになったことが最大の変化です。

segments.speaker: Moderator
segments.text: After another summer of record-breaking heat, several cities are experimenting with ways to reduce street temperatures. Urban planner Aisha Grant, where should cities begin?

segments.speaker: Aisha
segments.text: Shade. Trees are excellent because they cool through both shade and evaporation, but they need years to mature and they need water. In places where planting space is limited, awnings and covered walkways can provide faster relief.

segments.speaker: Moderator
segments.text: Dr Kim, you study reflective roofs. Are they a better solution?

segments.speaker: Kim
segments.text: They are one useful tool. A light-coloured roof absorbs less solar energy than a dark roof, which can reduce indoor temperatures and demand for air conditioning. But roof treatments do much less for pedestrians at street level unless they are part of a wider plan.

segments.speaker: Moderator
segments.text: Community organizer Rosa Mendes, what is missing from this conversation?

segments.speaker: Rosa
segments.text: Distribution. Cities often announce a total number of new trees, but the hottest neighbourhoods may have the least space, the oldest housing and the fewest residents able to pay for cooling. We need to ask who receives the benefit, not only how many projects are completed.

segments.speaker: Aisha
segments.text: I agree. We also have to maintain what we build. A young tree that dies after two summers is not a long-term cooling strategy.

segments.speaker: Kim
segments.text: And we should measure results. Surface temperature, indoor temperature and people's actual experience are different indicators. A project can improve one without improving all three.

segments.speaker: Moderator
segments.text: So the shared message is that heat adaptation needs several tools, long-term maintenance and careful attention to who benefits.

questions.prompt: Why does Aisha say awnings can be useful?
options: They can provide shade quickly where planting space is limited.
questions.explanationJa: treeが育つのを待てない場所や植樹スペースが少ない場所で、早くshadeを作れます。

questions.prompt: Give two benefits Kim associates with reflective roofs.
markscheme: They absorb less solar energy than dark roofs.
They can reduce indoor temperatures and/or reduce demand for air conditioning.
questions.explanationJa: solar energyの吸収を減らし、indoor temperatureやair-conditioning需要を下げられます。

questions.prompt: Choose TWO concerns Rosa raises about fairness.
options: The hottest neighbourhoods may have little planting space.
Every neighbourhood already has equal tree cover.
Cooling projects should only be private.
questions.explanationJa: hottest neighbourhoodsの植樹スペース不足とold housingを問題として挙げています。

questions.prompt: Aisha says cities must ________ what they build.
markscheme: maintain
questions.explanationJa: 作って終わりではなくmaintenanceが必要だと述べています。

questions.prompt: Matching task: Match each speaker to the main issue they emphasize: Rosa and Kim.
markscheme: Rosa — fair distribution / who receives the benefits.
Kim — measuring different outcomes / distinguishing surface, indoor and lived temperature effects.
questions.explanationJa: Rosaはequity、Kimはmeasurementとindicatorの違いを強調しています。

questions.prompt: What is the moderator's purpose in the final sentence?
options: To summarize the areas of agreement
To introduce a completely new technology
To argue that trees are the only solution
questions.explanationJa: 複数のtool、maintenance、benefit distributionという共通点をまとめています。

texts.title: When translation software meets a hospital

segments.speaker: Host
segments.text: Hospitals increasingly use digital translation tools at reception desks. Dr Meera Shah, where are these systems genuinely helpful?

segments.speaker: Shah
segments.text: They are useful for routine communication: confirming an address, explaining where a department is, or helping someone describe a simple administrative problem. They can reduce waiting time when a human interpreter is not immediately available.

segments.speaker: Host
segments.text: Where do you draw the line?

segments.speaker: Shah
segments.text: Anything involving consent, serious diagnosis, complex medication instructions or sensitive personal history should not depend on an automatic translation alone. A sentence can be grammatically accurate and still miss uncertainty, politeness or cultural meaning.

segments.speaker: Host
segments.text: Software developer Leo Martin, is that a criticism of the technology?

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: It is a criticism of using the technology outside its proper role. We are improving accuracy, but the product should also signal confidence. If the system is unsure, staff need to know that rather than receiving a smooth sentence that looks more reliable than it is.

segments.speaker: Shah
segments.text: Exactly. The safest design is not the one that pretends to replace interpreters. It is the one that helps staff recognize when an interpreter is necessary.

segments.speaker: Host
segments.text: So usefulness depends not only on what the software can do, but on whether users understand its limits.

questions.prompt: Which task does Shah consider suitable for translation software?
questions.explanationJa: routine communicationの例としてaddress確認を挙げています。

questions.prompt: Give two situations in which Shah says automatic translation should not be used alone.
markscheme: Consent and/or serious diagnosis.
Complex medication instructions and/or sensitive personal history.
questions.explanationJa: consent、serious diagnosis、medication instructions、sensitive historyなどから2点です。

questions.prompt: Leo says the product should signal its level of ________.
markscheme: confidence
questions.explanationJa: systemがどれほど確信しているかをstaffに示すべきだと述べています。

questions.prompt: Choose TWO ideas the speakers agree on.
options: Translation software can be useful for routine tasks.
Automatic translation should replace interpreters completely.
Users need to understand when the system may be unreliable.
Smooth wording always means an accurate translation.
Hospitals should avoid all digital tools.
questions.explanationJa: routine taskには有用ですが、限界や不確実性を理解する必要がある点で一致しています。

questions.prompt: What does Shah mean by the 'safest design'?
options: A system that helps staff know when human interpretation is needed
A system that translates only written signs
A system with the fastest possible response
questions.explanationJa: human interpreterが必要な場面を認識させる設計を指します。

questions.prompt: What is the host's final conclusion?
options: Accuracy is the only factor that matters.
The value of the tool depends partly on users understanding its limits.
questions.explanationJa: toolの能力だけでなく、利用者がlimitを理解しているかが重要だとまとめています。

segments.speaker: Reporter
segments.text: Three rural secondary schools will test a four-day teaching week next term. Students will attend longer classes from Monday to Thursday, while Friday will be used for optional study sessions, sports and teacher planning.

segments.speaker: Principal
segments.text: The proposal began because recruiting teachers has become difficult. We hope a different timetable will make the schools more attractive to staff, but we are treating this as a trial, not a permanent solution.

segments.speaker: Reporter
segments.text: Some parents support the experiment because older students already travel long distances by bus. One fewer compulsory journey could save time. Other parents worry about childcare, especially for younger teenagers whose parents work on Fridays.

segments.speaker: Parent
segments.text: My daughter is fourteen. An optional study session sounds useful, but optional services can disappear when budgets are tight. I want to know whether Friday supervision is guaranteed for families who need it.

segments.speaker: Reporter
segments.text: Teachers have also asked how longer days will affect concentration. The district says it will compare attendance, staff vacancies, student results and family surveys after two terms before deciding whether to continue.

questions.prompt: What will happen on Fridays during the trial?
options: Optional study, sports and teacher planning will take place.
Only teachers will attend normal lessons.
questions.explanationJa: Fridayはoptional study、sports、teacher planningに使われます。

questions.prompt: Give two reasons some people support the trial.
markscheme: It may help the schools recruit or retain teachers.
Students who travel long distances may make one fewer compulsory journey and save time.
questions.explanationJa: teacher recruitmentとlong-distance travelの負担軽減が主な賛成理由です。

questions.prompt: Choose TWO concerns mentioned in the report.
options: Childcare for families who work on Fridays
questions.explanationJa: Friday childcareとlonger dayでのconcentrationが懸念されています。

questions.prompt: The principal describes the change as a ________, not a permanent solution.
markscheme: trial
questions.explanationJa: 恒久制度ではなくtrialとして扱うと明言しています。

questions.prompt: What is the parent's attitude toward the optional Friday session?
options: Supportive but concerned that it may not be reliably available
Uninterested because her daughter is too young
Certain that it will reduce school costs
questions.explanationJa: usefulと認めつつ、budget次第で消える可能性を心配しています。

questions.prompt: Why will the district collect several different measures?
options: To judge the trial from multiple effects before deciding whether to continue
To rank the three schools publicly
To replace all family surveys with exam scores
To end the trial after one week
questions.explanationJa: attendance、staffing、results、family feedbackなど複数の影響を見て判断するためです。

segments.speaker: Moderator
segments.text: Our student panel is discussing school uniforms. Priya, what do you like about having one?

segments.speaker: Priya
segments.text: I like not deciding what to wear every morning. More importantly, when we visit another school for a competition, the uniform makes me feel part of a team. I know that sounds simple, but symbols can create belonging.

segments.speaker: Moderator
segments.text: Marcus, you see it differently.

segments.speaker: Marcus
segments.text: I understand the belonging argument, but rules often go far beyond a basic uniform. Hair, jewellery, shoes and even small badges can become tightly controlled. At that point the school is not only asking students to dress similarly; it is deciding which forms of self-expression are acceptable.

segments.speaker: Priya
segments.text: That's a fair criticism. I would keep the core uniform but allow more flexibility around accessories and hairstyles, provided there is a clear safety reason for any restriction.

segments.speaker: Moderator
segments.text: Amina, what matters most to you?

segments.speaker: Amina
segments.text: Cost. People talk about identity, but a uniform policy also affects families' budgets. If a school requires one expensive supplier, a supposedly equal uniform can create inequality. Second-hand exchanges and generic items matter.

segments.speaker: Marcus
segments.text: I agree with Amina. A policy can look equal because everyone wears the same thing while still placing very different pressure on different families.

segments.speaker: Moderator
segments.text: So the debate is not simply uniform or no uniform. It is about belonging, expression, safety and affordability, and how those priorities are balanced.

questions.prompt: What benefit does Priya associate with uniforms during competitions?
options: They create a sense of belonging to a team.
questions.explanationJa: uniformがteamへのbelongingを感じさせると述べています。

questions.prompt: Give two examples Marcus uses of rules that may restrict self-expression.
markscheme: Hair and/or jewellery rules.
Shoe and/or badge rules.
questions.explanationJa: hair、jewellery、shoes、badgesなどから2つ挙げればよい問題です。

questions.prompt: How does Priya respond to Marcus's criticism?
options: She changes her position to oppose uniforms entirely.
She accepts part of it and supports flexibility beyond the core uniform.
She says safety can never justify a restriction.
questions.explanationJa: 批判を一部認め、core uniform以外には柔軟性を持たせる立場です。

questions.prompt: Choose TWO measures Amina suggests could reduce financial pressure.
questions.explanationJa: second-hand exchangeとgeneric itemsを提案しています。

questions.prompt: Matching task: Match each speaker to their main emphasis: Priya and Amina.
markscheme: Priya — belonging / team identity (while accepting some flexibility).
Amina — affordability / unequal financial pressure on families.
questions.explanationJa: Priyaはbelonging、Aminaはcostとfinancial inequalityが中心です。

questions.prompt: What is the moderator's main purpose at the end?
options: To announce a new uniform rule
To show that the issue involves several competing priorities
To prove that Marcus has won the debate
To argue that cost is the only important issue
questions.explanationJa: uniformの是非を二択にせず、複数のpriorityのbalanceとしてまとめています。

segments.speaker: Host
segments.text: Actor and student Jamie Cole joined an improvisation club after years of avoiding public performance. Jamie, why improvisation?

segments.speaker: Jamie
segments.text: Because it frightened me. In prepared presentations I could memorize every sentence. Improvisation removes that safety net. You have to respond to what another person gives you, and sometimes your idea simply does not work.

segments.speaker: Host
segments.text: That sounds stressful rather than educational.

segments.speaker: Jamie
segments.text: At first it was. Then I noticed that experienced performers failed constantly, but they did not freeze. They acknowledged what happened and built the next moment from it. The audience usually forgot the mistake faster than the performer did.

segments.speaker: Host
segments.text: Did that affect you outside the club?

segments.speaker: Jamie
segments.text: Yes. I now ask questions in class sooner instead of waiting until I can phrase them perfectly. I also recover faster if a presentation goes off plan. I still prepare carefully; I just no longer expect preparation to remove every uncertainty.

segments.speaker: Host
segments.text: So the lesson is to stop preparing?

segments.speaker: Jamie
segments.text: Definitely not. The lesson is that preparation and adaptability are partners. Preparation gives you material to work with; adaptability helps when reality refuses to follow the script.

questions.prompt: Why did Jamie choose improvisation?
options: It challenged a fear of unplanned public performance.
questions.explanationJa: 自分が怖れていたunplanned performanceにあえて挑戦するためでした。

questions.prompt: Give two things Jamie observed about experienced performers when mistakes happened.
markscheme: They failed regularly but did not freeze.
They acknowledged the mistake and built the next moment from it.
questions.explanationJa: 失敗しても止まらず、その出来事を次の展開に利用していました。

questions.prompt: Jamie says the audience often forgot a mistake faster than the ________ did.
markscheme: performer
questions.explanationJa: performer本人の方が失敗を長く気にしているという意味です。

questions.prompt: Choose TWO changes Jamie noticed outside the club.
options: Recovering faster when presentations go off plan
questions.explanationJa: classで早く質問することと、presentationの崩れから早くrecoverすることです。

questions.prompt: What is Jamie's attitude toward preparation?
options: Preparation remains important but must be combined with adaptability.
questions.explanationJa: preparationを否定せず、adaptabilityと組み合わせるべきだと考えています。

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of the interview?
options: To explain how an uncomfortable experience changed Jamie's response to uncertainty
To argue that mistakes should be ignored completely
questions.explanationJa: improvisation経験を通じてuncertaintyへの向き合い方が変化したことが中心です。

segments.speaker: Reporter
segments.text: A city stadium that once sold more than twenty thousand single-use water bottles during major events has installed twelve refill stations and changed its entry rules so spectators may bring empty reusable bottles.

segments.speaker: Manager
segments.text: The environmental case was obvious, but convenience mattered just as much. If people had to walk across the stadium or queue for ten minutes, they would simply buy another disposable bottle. So we studied where crowds actually moved before choosing locations.

segments.speaker: Reporter
segments.text: The first month revealed an unexpected problem: several stations were busiest immediately after security checks, while machines near the upper seating areas were barely used.

segments.speaker: Manager
segments.text: We moved two stations and added clearer signs. We also changed the water pressure because filling a large bottle was taking too long. Small details can decide whether a sustainable option feels normal or inconvenient.

segments.speaker: Reporter
segments.text: Sales of disposable water bottles fell by sixty-two percent during the trial, but they did not disappear. The stadium kept some bottles for emergencies and for visitors who arrived without a reusable container.

segments.speaker: Manager
segments.text: Our next question is waste beyond water. Food packaging is more complicated because hygiene and different vendors are involved. We want to avoid claiming success in one area while ignoring the rest of the event.

questions.prompt: What rule changed when the refill stations were installed?
options: Spectators may bring empty reusable bottles.
questions.explanationJa: empty reusable bottleの持ち込みが認められるようになりました。

questions.prompt: Why did the stadium study crowd movement before placing refill stations? Give two linked ideas.
markscheme: Convenience would affect whether spectators used the refill option.
Long walks or queues could cause people to buy disposable bottles instead.
questions.explanationJa: 利用しやすさが行動に影響し、不便ならdisposable bottleに戻るからです。

questions.prompt: Choose TWO changes made after the first month.
questions.explanationJa: station移動とsign改善が行われました。

questions.prompt: Disposable water-bottle sales fell by ________ percent during the trial.
markscheme: 62 (sixty-two)
questions.explanationJa: trial中の減少率は62 percentです。

questions.prompt: Why did the stadium keep some disposable bottles?
options: For emergencies and visitors without reusable containers.
questions.explanationJa: emergencyとreusable containerを持たないvisitorへの対応です。

questions.prompt: What concern does the manager express at the end?
options: Water waste is the only environmental issue.
The stadium should not celebrate one improvement while ignoring other waste.
Food vendors should all be removed.
Reusable bottles create more waste than packaging.
questions.explanationJa: waterだけの成果で満足せず、food packagingなど他のwasteも見る必要があると述べています。

segments.speaker: Moderator
segments.text: Several platforms now test labels for images or audio that may have been generated or heavily altered by artificial intelligence. Researcher Elena Price, what can a label realistically achieve?

segments.speaker: Elena
segments.text: A label can create a moment of caution. It tells the viewer not to assume that a realistic-looking clip is a direct record of an event. But a label is only useful if people understand what it means and if genuine content is not incorrectly labelled too often.

segments.speaker: Moderator
segments.text: Journalist Ben Okafor, are you convinced?

segments.speaker: Ben
segments.text: Partly. My concern is timing. False material can spread to millions of people before a platform reviews it. A correct label added two days later may help the archive, but it does not undo the first wave of attention.

segments.speaker: Moderator
segments.text: Digital artist Mei Tan, creators sometimes object to these systems.

segments.speaker: Mei
segments.text: Yes, because 'AI-generated' can sound like 'deceptive' even when a creator openly uses AI as one tool in an artwork. We need more precise categories. There is a difference between an invented news clip designed to mislead and an illustrated poster that clearly presents itself as fiction.

segments.speaker: Elena
segments.text: That is why provenance matters too. Instead of relying only on a warning added after publication, we can attach information about where a file came from and what edits were made. No single system will solve the trust problem.

segments.speaker: Ben
segments.text: And audiences still need verification habits. Technology can provide signals, but people must compare sources, check dates and ask who benefits from a claim.

segments.speaker: Moderator
segments.text: So all three of you support more information, but you differ on what labels can accomplish by themselves.

questions.prompt: According to Elena, what is one useful effect of a label?
options: It proves every clip is false.
It creates a moment of caution before viewers trust realistic-looking material.
It prevents all altered media from being uploaded.
It replaces the need to understand context.
questions.explanationJa: viewerに一度立ち止まって疑うmoment of cautionを作ることができます。

questions.prompt: Give two conditions Elena says affect whether labels are useful.
markscheme: People need to understand what the label means.
Genuine content should not be incorrectly labelled too often.
questions.explanationJa: labelの意味が理解されることと、false positiveが多すぎないことが必要です。

questions.prompt: What is Ben's main concern about platform labels?
options: They may be added only after false material has already spread widely.
They are too easy for artists to read.
questions.explanationJa: labelが付くまでにmisinformationが広く拡散してしまうtimingの問題です。

questions.prompt: Choose TWO distinctions or actions mentioned in the discussion.
options: Distinguish deceptive fake news from openly fictional creative work.
Assume every AI-assisted artwork is deceptive.
Trust any clip without a label.
questions.explanationJa: Meiのcategory distinctionとBenのsource/date verificationが正しいです。

questions.prompt: Matching task: Match each speaker to the concern they emphasize: Ben and Mei.
markscheme: Ben — timing / labels may arrive after misinformation has already spread.
Mei — overly broad labels can wrongly imply deception and should distinguish types of AI use.
questions.explanationJa: Benはtiming、Meiはlabelの意味が広すぎることを問題視しています。

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the panel's overall position?
options: Labels alone will solve online trust problems.
No information about edited media should be shown.
More information is useful, but labels need other forms of provenance and verification.
Only journalists should be allowed to use AI tools.
questions.explanationJa: label単独では不十分で、provenanceやverification habitsと組み合わせる必要があるという結論です。
